name: Chinese nail staining

lead: Nail colouring in China is traced by Wikipedia to about 3000 BCE, and in the Zhou dynasty (c. 600 BCE) royal houses favoured gold and silver, later replaced by red and black. Colour on the nails signalled status, so tinted nails were part of a refined appearance.
In the Ming dynasty, nail lacquers were reportedly made from beeswax, egg white, gelatin, vegetable dyes and gum arabic.

paras: Practitioners applied the coloured mixture to the nails and let it set. Colour choice marked rank rather than only taste.
Little documented. Modern case reports describe nail discolouration from hydroquinone creams, a different phenomenon.

chain: Groomed hands and a rank signal
angle.text: Coloured nails gave hands a finished look and, in dynastic China, signalled rank through permitted colours.

lead: Chinese nail staining refers to the early Chinese practice of colouring the nails, which Wikipedia dates to about 3000 BCE.[1] Coloured nails gave hands a groomed look and, according to the account, carried class meaning.[1]

During the Zhou dynasty (about 600 BCE) the royal house favoured gold and silver, with red and black later becoming royal preferences, so nail colour tracked social rank.[1] In the Ming dynasty nail polish was often made from beeswax, egg whites, gelatin, vegetable dyes and gum arabic.[1]

paras: Nail polish has origins in China dating back to roughly 3000 BCE.[1] Zhou royalty favoured metallic and then red and black shades, tying colour to rank.[1] Ming recipes combined beeswax, egg white, gelatin, vegetable dye and gum arabic.[1]
No studies found. Dermatology case reports describe accidental nail staining from hydroquinone skin-lightening cream, which resolved after stopping it, but these concern a different cause.[2][3]
